title: Claisen condensation
subtitle: Two molecules of ethyl acetate give ethyl acetoacetate

reactants.caption: ethyl acetate + sodium ethoxide
reactants.learnerPrompt: Ethoxide is the base. Form the ester enolate.
hintTiers: A C–H next to a C=O group is acidic: its conjugate base puts the negative charge on oxygen. The α-protons of an ester have a pKa of about 25.
Ethoxide takes one of the drawn hydrogens on the CH₃ group. That C–H pair forms a C=C bond to the carbonyl carbon, and the C=O π pair moves onto oxygen. Three arrows.
Ethoxide lone pair → new bond to a drawn hydrogen; that C–H bond → a π bond to the carbonyl carbon; the C=O π bond → a lone pair on the carbonyl oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Ethoxide does add to the ester carbonyl, but losing ethoxide again just gives back ethyl acetate: nothing changes. Here ethoxide acts as a base.
The C=O π electrons go to the electronegative oxygen, not onto the carbon that already shares them.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Good: ethoxide takes the proton and a C=C bond forms. The carbonyl carbon now has five bonds: move the C=O π pair onto oxygen.

enolate-and-ester.caption: ester enolate + a second ethyl acetate
enolate-and-ester.learnerPrompt: The enolate attacks the second ester.
hintTiers: The enolate is a carbon nucleophile. Which atom of the second ester is electron-poor?
The O⁻ lone pair pushes back in to re-form C=O, the C=C π pair forms a new C–C bond to the other ester's carbonyl carbon, and that C=O π pair moves onto its oxygen. Three arrows.
Enolate O⁻ lone pair → C=O π bond; C=C π bond → new C–C bond to the carbonyl carbon of the second ester; its C=O π bond → a lone pair on its oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: The enolate oxygen can attack, but that gives nothing useful and is reversible. The Claisen makes a C–C bond: attack with the α-carbon.
The carbonyl oxygen is electron-rich. The electrophile is the carbonyl carbon.
A methyl carbon has no leaving group and no π bond: it is not an electrophile. Attack the carbonyl carbon.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right bonds, but this leaves a positive carbon next to O⁻ on the enolate side. Push the O⁻ lone pair in to re-form C=O.

tetrahedral-intermediate.caption: tetrahedral intermediate + ethanol
hintTiers: An alkoxide on a carbon that also carries an OEt group can re-form C=O. Which group leaves?
The O⁻ lone pair re-forms the C=O π bond and the C–OEt bond breaks, the pair going to the ethoxy oxygen. Two arrows.
O⁻ lone pair → C=O π bond; C–OEt bond → a lone pair on that oxygen (ethoxide leaves).

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Breaking the new C–C bond just gives back the enolate and the ester. Let ethoxide leave instead.
A methyl anion is a hopeless leaving group. Ethoxide, the conjugate base of an alcohol, leaves.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Ethoxide does leave, but only when pushed. Add the arrow from the O⁻ lone pair re-forming C=O.

keto-ester.caption: ethyl acetoacetate (a β-keto ester) + ethoxide + ethanol
keto-ester.learnerPrompt: Ethoxide removes the most acidic proton in the flask.
hintTiers: Every step so far is uphill or reversible. Which C–H is flanked by two C=O groups?
Ethoxide takes the drawn hydrogen on the CH₂ between the ketone and the ester. The C–H pair forms a C=C bond to the ketone carbon, and that C=O π pair moves onto oxygen. Three arrows.
Ethoxide lone pair → new bond to the drawn hydrogen; that C–H bond → a π bond to the ketone carbon; the ketone C=O π bond → a lone pair on its oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Ethoxide can add to a carbonyl group again, but that only runs the reaction backwards. The CH₂ between two C=O groups (pKa about 11) is far more acidic than ethanol (pKa 16): take that proton.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Good: ethoxide takes the proton between the two carbonyl groups. The ketone carbon now has five bonds: move its C=O π pair onto oxygen.

stabilised-enolate.caption: the enolate of ethyl acetoacetate + ethanol

enolate-and-acid.caption: the enolate of ethyl acetoacetate + H₃O⁺ (work-up)
enolate-and-acid.learnerPrompt: Acid work-up: put a proton back on the central carbon.
hintTiers: The enolate is a base. Which species is the acid, and which atom gives the keto form?
The C=C π pair takes a proton from H₃O⁺, the O–H pair stays on water's oxygen, and the O⁻ lone pair re-forms C=O. Three arrows.
C=C π bond → new C–H bond to a proton of H₃O⁺; that O–H bond → a lone pair on water's oxygen; enolate O⁻ lone pair → C=O π bond.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Protonating oxygen gives the enol, which then tautomerises to the keto ester. Put the proton on the central carbon to reach the keto form directly.
Protonating an oxygen gives an enol. Put the proton on the central carbon to reach the keto ester directly.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: the central carbon takes the proton. That leaves a positive carbon next to O⁻: push the O⁻ lone pair in to re-form C=O.

steps.explanationAfterStep: Ethoxide (pKa of ethanol 16) is too weak to deprotonate the ester (pKa about 25) completely: only a small amount of enolate is present at any moment. That is enough.

steps.caption: Most of the ester is not deprotonated: a second molecule of ethyl acetate meets the enolate.

steps.explanationAfterStep: The new C–C bond. Unlike the aldol, the alkoxide sits on a carbon that still carries a leaving group.
Addition then elimination, as for any ester: ethoxide leaves and a ketone forms. These steps are all reversible, and the equilibrium does not favour the β-keto ester.

This is why the Claisen works. The CH₂ between two C=O groups (pKa about 11) is much more acidic than ethanol, so this proton transfer is strongly downhill and pulls every earlier equilibrium over. A full equivalent of ethoxide is used up.

steps.caption: Ethanol is left out of the drawing. Dilute aqueous acid is added at the end (work-up).

steps.explanationAfterStep: The acid neutralises the enolate. The acid must come only at the end: during the reaction the enolate salt is the product.

mechanismSummary: Ethoxide removes an α-proton from ethyl acetate. The ester enolate adds to a second ester molecule, and the tetrahedral intermediate loses ethoxide to give a β-keto ester. Ethoxide then removes the proton between the two carbonyl groups: this irreversible step drives the whole sequence and uses up a full equivalent of base. Acid work-up gives ethyl acetoacetate.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 26
